query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition due to their unique multi-principal-element compositions, which give rise to the high-entropy effect, severe lattice distortion effect, sluggish diffusion effect, and cocktail effect.
generation.intervention: Adjusting the composition of the high-entropy alloy, such as changing the ratio of elements or adding new elements
generation.mechanism: The high-entropy effect, severe lattice distortion effect, sluggish diffusion effect, and cocktail effect interact to influence the mechanical properties of the alloy, including its ductility and brittleness
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved ductility and resistance to brittleness in high-entropy alloys
generation.baseline: Conventional alloys with limited ductility and high brittleness
generation.boundary: The optimal composition and processing conditions for high-entropy alloys to achieve ductile–brittle–ductile transition
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanisms by which the high-entropy effect, severe lattice distortion effect, sluggish diffusion effect, and cocktail effect influence the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys are not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: Systematic variation of composition and processing conditions to test the effects on ductility and brittleness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy does not exhibit improved ductility and resistance to brittleness under varied conditions, the hypothesis is falsified

System: (CoNi)50(TiZrHf)50 (at. %) single-phase B2 high-entropy intermetallic alloy. Processing: Arc-melting high-purity raw materials (>99.9 wt.%) under Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, remelted at least five times, drop-cast into a copper mold, homogenized at 1000 °C for 24 h, and water quenched. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), including CoCrFeMnNi, CoCrFeNi, FeCuCrMnMo, and CoCrNi medium-entropy alloys. Processing: Various methods, including vacuum arc melting (VAM), additive manufacturing (AM) techniques such as selective laser melting (SLM), electron beam melting (EBM), and Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF). Test conditions: Hydrogen charging, tensile testing, and microstructural analysis. System: FeCoNi(AlSi)x where x ranges from 0 to 0.8 in molar ratio (alloys denoted A0 to A8). System: 614 reported HEAs (Level 3) and 42 newly synthesized complex compositions containing 4 to 7 elements from refractory metals, transition metals, and main group elements (e.g., Al2CoCrCuNi). Paper card. Question: How can a strong and ductile medium-entropy alloy be designed to resist hydrogen embrittlement and corrosion?. System: CoNiV medium-entropy alloy with face-centered cubic structure. Processing: Vacuum induction melting, drop-casting, homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 h, cold-rolling to 75% thickness reduction, and recrystallization annealing at 950 °C for 1 h. Test conditions: Slow strain rate tensile testing at 10−4 s−1, hydrogen charging at 50 mA cm−2 in 0.5 M H2SO4 solution, and corrosion testing in 0.1 M H2SO4 solution. Findings: The CoNiV MEA shows high resistance to hydrogen embrittlement at ambient temperature; The alloy has a low hydrogen diffusivity of ~10−13 m2 s−1; The formation of a dense oxide film on the alloy surface reduces the hydrogen uptake rate and provides high corrosion resistance; The alloy exhibits a good strength-ductility relation combined with high resistance to corrosion; The total elongation drops by only ~1.5% in the presence of hydrogen; The corrosion current density remains below 7 μA cm−2.
